y-m-30-01.title: Is the triangle with sides 8, 15, 17 a right triangle?
y-m-30-01.topic: The converse of the Pythagorean theorem and right triangles whose side lengths are natural numbers
y-m-30-01.goal: Check which side is taken as the longest side when checking for a right triangle, find right triangles with natural-number sides of different kinds, and explain what 'the same kind' means.
y-m-30-01.material: Minseo measured the three sides of a triangle-shaped decoration and got 8 cm, 15 cm, and 17 cm. She did not measure any angles and only knows the three side lengths. To check whether this triangle is a right triangle, Minseo calculated as below. (All units of length are cm. 8² is read as 'eight squared' and 17² as 'seventeen squared'.)
y-m-30-01.thinking.0: Finding the position of an error in a calculation process
y-m-30-01.thinking.1: Making several examples under constraints (natural numbers, a limit on the hypotenuse, excluding enlargements)
y-m-30-01.thinking.2: Setting a standard for a 'new example'
y-m-30-01.prereq.1: In a right triangle, the relation between the sum of the squares of two sides and the square of the remaining side, and that its converse holds (grade 9 level)
y-m-30-01.prereq.2: Divisors and the greatest common divisor
y-m-30-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose the one wrong line in Minseo's calculation. Count the line numbers from 1.
y-m-30-01.s.s1.hint.0: Do the same kind of calculation with the known right triangle 3, 4, 5. If you take 3 and 5 as the sides forming the right angle and compare 3²+5² with 4², what happens?
y-m-30-01.s.s1.hint.1: After checking where the longest of the three sides is in the case of 3, 4, 5, compare whether the two sides Minseo chose are in the same position.
y-m-30-01.s.s1.line.0: The lengths of the three sides are 8, 15, 17.
y-m-30-01.s.s1.line.1: I do not know which side is the hypotenuse, so let me take 8 and 17 as the two sides forming the right angle and calculate.
y-m-30-01.s.s1.line.3: 353 ≠ 225, so this triangle is not a right triangle.
y-m-30-01.s.s1.explain: Line 2 is the problem. If it is a right triangle, the side opposite the right angle (the hypotenuse) is the longest, so the longest side 17 must be the side compared with 'the sum of the squares of the other two sides'. If you take 17 as a side forming the right angle and compare, it is hard for it to hold for any triangle. So the conclusion in line 4 cannot be trusted either. Calculating correctly, 8²+15²=64+225=289=17², so it is a right triangle.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 right triangles of different kinds in which all three sides a, b, c are natural numbers (c is the hypotenuse). Conditions: the hypotenuse c is 30 or less, and the greatest common divisor of the three sides is 1. (Writing a and b in the other order gives the same triangle.)
y-m-30-01.s.s2.hint.0: Start from the already known 3, 4, 5, and change one of the two shorter sides to see whether the remaining side becomes a natural number.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.hint.1: First check whether the triangle you found is one in the list enlarged at the same ratio, and whether all three sides are divisible by the same number.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The three sides are natural numbers.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.fail.c1: All three sides must be natural numbers 1 or more.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the squares of two sides equals the square of the hypotenuse.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.fail.c2: a²+b² is not equal to c². Check again whether the hypotenuse is right.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.fail.c3: The hypotenuse c must be 30 or less.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.ok.c4: The greatest common divisor of the three sides is 1.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.fail.c4: The three sides have a common divisor greater than 1. It may be an enlargement of a smaller triangle.
y-m-30-01.s.s2.explain: The triangles that satisfy the conditions are only the five (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), (7, 24, 25), (20, 21, 29) (you can check them directly). (6, 8, 10) is excluded because the greatest common divisor is 2.
y-m-30-01.s.s3.prompt: Write in your own words why (6, 8, 10) is not counted as a 'new triangle' different from (3, 4, 5).
y-m-30-01.s.s3.hint.0: Pair up the corresponding side lengths of the two triangles one by one and write whether there is a division or multiplication relationship.
y-m-30-01.s.s3.hint.1: First write in one sentence which has changed, 'size' or 'shape'.
y-m-30-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you show the relationship between 3, 4, 5 and 6, 8, 10 with numbers?
y-m-30-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you distinguish which of 'shape' and 'size' is the same and which is different?
y-m-30-01.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say that all three sides grew by the same ratio?
y-m-30-01.s.s3.model.0: 6, 8, 10 is 3, 4, 5 each multiplied by 2, so it is a triangle with the same shape. Only the size is different, so I did not count it as a new kind.
y-m-30-01.s.s3.model.1: All three sides are the same multiple of 3, 4, 5, so it is an enlargement of the 3, 4, 5 triangle (a similar triangle). So I counted it as the same kind.

y-m-30-02.title: Estimating the height of a flagpole from an angle of elevation of 35°
y-m-30-02.topic: Using trigonometric ratios (finding a height from an angle of elevation)
y-m-30-02.goal: Learn that an angle of elevation alone does not determine the height, choose what more information is needed, check that the eye height must be added, and guess the effect that error in measuring the angle has on the result.
y-m-30-02.material: You want to find the height of the flagpole on the school playground. The ground is flat and the flagpole is perpendicular to the ground. Standing at a place away from the flagpole and looking up at the top, you measured the angle looking up (the angle of elevation) and it was 35°. You have not measured any other values yet. Reference: tan 35° is about 0.7002, sin 35° is about 0.5736, and cos 35° is about 0.8192. 'tan' is read as 'tangent'.
y-m-30-02.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-30-02.thinking.1: Finding different combinations of information that lead to the same result
y-m-30-02.thinking.2: Estimating the effect of measurement error on the result
y-m-30-02.prereq.0: The meaning of the trigonometric ratios (sine, cosine, tangent) of an angle in a right triangle
y-m-30-02.prereq.1: Reading a table of values of trigonometric ratios or using the given approximate values
y-m-30-02.s.s1.prompt: You have found out only the angle of elevation of 35°. What more do you need to know to determine the height of the flagpole? Choose everything that is necessary. (There may be different fitting combinations.)
y-m-30-02.s.s1.hint.0: Describe in words the right triangle that the angle of elevation makes. From which point to which point is each side?
y-m-30-02.s.s1.hint.1: Among the sides of that triangle, separate the ones you already know from the ones you do not, and also check whether the height starts from the ground or from the eyes.
y-m-30-02.s.s1.o.a: The horizontal distance 20 m from where you stand to the bottom of the flagpole
y-m-30-02.s.s1.r.a: With the horizontal distance, together with the angle of elevation, you can determine the height risen from the eyes to the top.
y-m-30-02.s.s1.o.b: The straight-line distance from the eyes to the top, about 24.4 m
y-m-30-02.s.s1.r.b: The straight-line distance, paired with the angle of elevation, also lets you determine the height. However, it is hard to measure directly.
y-m-30-02.s.s1.o.c: The height from the ground to the eyes, 1.5 m
y-m-30-02.s.s1.r.c: If you find only the height above the eyes, it is not the height from the ground to the top. Think about from where to where the height is.
y-m-30-02.s.s1.o.d: The thickness of the flagpole, about 10 cm
y-m-30-02.s.s1.r.d: The thickness is information unrelated to the height of the top. Think about whether it is a length that enters the triangle that determines the height.
y-m-30-02.s.s1.explain: To find the height above the eyes from the angle of elevation, you need one more length (the horizontal distance or the straight-line distance). Also, that height is from the eyes to the top, so to find the height from the ground to the top, you must add the eye height.
y-m-30-02.s.s1.acc.0: Even if you know the straight-line distance from the eyes to the top, together with the angle of elevation you can determine the height above the eyes, and then you add the eye height. However, it is hard to measure the straight-line distance directly, so using the horizontal distance is more realistic.
y-m-30-02.s.s2.prompt: Now you have measured the horizontal distance 20 m and the eye height 1.5 m. What is the most fitting value for the height of the flagpole? (tan 35° ≈ 0.7002)
y-m-30-02.s.s2.hint.0: In the right triangle that has the angle of elevation as one angle, decide whether 20 m and the height you want to find are the side adjacent to that angle and the side opposite it.
y-m-30-02.s.s2.hint.1: After checking whether the height you found is from the eyes or from the ground, adjust it appropriately.
y-m-30-02.s.s2.r.a: You may have used a different trigonometric ratio, with the horizontal distance as the adjacent side, to find the height above the eyes. Check again which side to which side the ratio is.
y-m-30-02.s.s2.r.b: You may have found only the height above the eyes and not added the eye height. Check again where the height starts.
y-m-30-02.s.s2.r.c: This is a solution that found the height from the ratio of the horizontal distance and the height above the eyes and then added the eye height.
y-m-30-02.s.s2.r.d: You may have used a trigonometric ratio that does not fit the relation between the horizontal distance and the height. Check again what the known side and the side you want to find each are.
y-m-30-02.s.s2.explain: The height above the eyes is 20×tan 35° ≈ 20×0.7002 ≈ 14.0 m, and adding the eye height 1.5 m gives about 15.5 m.
y-m-30-02.s.s3.prompt: The tool for measuring the angle of elevation has error, so the real angle of elevation could be 34° or 36°. How does the calculation of the flagpole height change then? Write using at least one number, and add one line on how much you can trust 15.5 m. (Reference: tan 34° ≈ 0.6745, tan 36° ≈ 0.7265)
y-m-30-02.s.s3.hint.0: Calculate the cases of 34° and 36° in the same order as at first.
y-m-30-02.s.s3.hint.1: Compare with the value at 35° and check how much they differ by subtracting.
y-m-30-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate and compare the heights at 34° and 36° directly?
y-m-30-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say with numbers how much the height changes even if the angle is off by only 1°?
y-m-30-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you try stating the result as a range, like 'between about so many m and so many m'?
y-m-30-02.s.s3.model.0: At 34°, 20×0.6745+1.5≈15.0 m, and at 36°, 20×0.7265+1.5≈16.0 m, so even if the angle is off by only 1°, the height changes by about 0.5 m. So it is good to trust 15.5 m as roughly 15 to 16 m.
y-m-30-02.s.s3.model.1: If measured as 36°, it is about 16.0 m, and if measured as 34°, it is about 15.0 m, so there is a difference of about 1 m. It is important to measure the angle of elevation accurately, and 15.5 m is a rough value.

y-m-30-03.title: Estimating the distance from a point outside a circle to the point of tangency
y-m-30-03.topic: The relation between a tangent of a circle and its radius
y-m-30-03.goal: Go through the process in which the length of a tangent, which at first could only be given as a range, becomes determined when the information that the tangent is perpendicular to the radius is added, and judge whether the same reasoning applies to a second tangent.
y-m-30-03.material: There is a circle O with radius 5 cm. From a point P outside the circle, draw a tangent to the circle, and call the point of tangency A. The distance from the center O to the point P is 13 cm. You want to find the length of the tangent PA. (There is no figure. Picture the triangle that has the three points O, A, P as its vertices.)
y-m-30-03.thinking.0: Seeing how the range and confidence of a judgment change as information grows
y-m-30-03.thinking.1: Telling an intuitive calculation (13 − 5) apart from a calculation with a basis
y-m-30-03.thinking.2: Judging whether it is fine to extend to another case with the same structure
y-m-30-03.prereq.0: The relation between the sum of the lengths of two sides of a triangle and the length of the remaining side
y-m-30-03.prereq.1: The fact that a tangent of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of tangency (it appears as new information in step 3)
y-m-30-03.prereq.2: The relation among the three sides of a right triangle
y-m-30-03.s.s1.prompt: Information is revealed one piece at a time. Judge using only the information up to that step, and you may revise your judgment after seeing the next information.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, first write in one sentence 'what was newly revealed', and then choose.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.info: What you know now: OA = 5 cm (radius), OP = 13 cm. Point A is a point on the circle and PA is a tangent of this circle. Do not use the property of tangents yet.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.ask: What can you say about the length of PA?
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.after: If O, A, P are not on one line, triangle OAP is formed. In a triangle, the sum of two sides is greater than the remaining side, so PA is greater than 13 − 5 = 8 and less than 13 + 5 = 18. 8 is the shortest distance from point P to the circle, and it is not the length of the tangent. For now you can only state a range.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You may have mixed up the shortest distance from point P to the circle with the length of the tangent. Think about whether point A is the position that makes this distance.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Longer than 8 cm and shorter than 18 cm
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that precisely derived the range of the length from the fact that the three points form a triangle.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.r.c: Think about whether there is a reason for taking OP and PA as the same length.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The value cannot be determined from this information alone
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.0.r.d: This is a careful judgment that considers that the exact value is not yet determined.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.1.info: New information: a tangent is perpendicular to the radius through the point of tangency. That is, OA ⊥ PA (the two segments form a right angle).
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.1.ask: Taking this information into account, what can you say about PA?
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.1.after: Triangle OAP is a right triangle with a right angle at A and its hypotenuse is OP. So PA² = 13² − 5² = 144, and PA = 12 cm. 12 lies between 8 and 18, so the first judgment of the range was not wrong, and the new information narrowed that range down to one value.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.1.o.a: The first judgment as it is: longer than 8 cm and shorter than 18 cm
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.1.r.a: The judgment of the range is still true. But think about whether it can be narrowed further with the new information.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You may have added the two squares without checking whether OP is a side forming the right angle or the hypotenuse.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You may have kept 8 without using the information that the tangent is perpendicular to the radius.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This is the value that used the point that the hypotenuse in the right triangle OAP is OP.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.info: Draw one more tangent from point P to the circle and call the point of tangency B (B is a different point from A). Minjun says, 'PB is also 12 cm,' and Seoa says, 'B is a different point from A, so PB might not be 12.'
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is the more valid statement about PB?
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.after: In triangle OBP too, OB = 5 (radius), OP = 13, and the angle at B is a right angle, so PB² = 169 − 25 = 144, and PB = 12 cm. The fact that the point of tangency is different has changed, but the conditions that determine the length (radius 5, distance to the center 13, right angle) are the same, so the value is the same.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.o.a: Seoa's statement is valid. If the point of tangency is different, the length can be different too
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This is a feeling that if the point of tangency changes, the value will change too. Think about what exactly is changing.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.o.b: There is no information, so neither statement can be judged
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You considered that there is no newly added information. Think about whether there are known values in triangle OBP.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Minjun's statement is valid. Triangle OBP has the same conditions
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This is a judgment that gave the reason that the two triangles have the same conditions.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.o.d: The two tangents have the same length, but you have to draw a figure to be sure
y-m-30-03.s.s1.st.2.r.d: The conclusion is the same, but think about whether a figure is really needed.
y-m-30-03.s.s1.reflect: In step 1 you could only state a range, and the new information in step 2 determined the value. Distinguish whether the first judgment of the range became 'wrong' because of the new information or was 'narrowed'. Also look back at whether in step 3 you judged by separating what changed (the point of tangency) from what did not change (the conditions that determine the length).
y-m-30-03.s.s2.prompt: A friend said, 'PA is 13 − 5 = 8 cm.' Explain to this friend, using numbers, why 8 cm is not the length of the tangent.
y-m-30-03.s.s2.hint.0: Say what 8 cm is the length of, using the positional relation between point P and the circle.
y-m-30-03.s.s2.hint.1: Write the process of finding PA using the property of tangents and the shape of triangle OAP.
y-m-30-03.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Did you say what the value 8 represents (the shortest distance from P to the circle)?
y-m-30-03.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you explain the shape of the triangle that determines the length of the tangent?
y-m-30-03.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you show the process by which the number I chose actually becomes 12?
y-m-30-03.s.s2.model.0: 13−5=8 is the nearest distance from point P to the circle. The tangent PA is perpendicular to the radius OA, so triangle OAP is a right triangle and its hypotenuse is OP=13, so PA=12 cm.
y-m-30-03.s.s2.model.1: PA must be longer than 8. In triangle OAP, adding 5 and 8 gives 13, so a triangle is not formed. In a right triangle, 13 is the longest side, so it becomes 12.

y-m-30-04.title: Is the angle that sees the diameter AB always 90° wherever point C is?
y-m-30-04.topic: The inscribed angle on a diameter and the position of a point
y-m-30-04.goal: Learn that 'the inscribed angle on a semicircle is 90°' is a property for when point C is on the circle, and use examples you make yourself to check and say what changes when a point inside or outside the circle sees the same angle.
y-m-30-04.material: On the coordinate plane, the center of circle O is the origin and the two endpoints of the diameter AB are A(−5, 0) and B(5, 0). The radius of the circle is 5, and point C is at a place where the y-coordinate is greater than 0. Hyejin used the fact that 'the inscribed angle on a semicircle is 90°' to say, '∠ACB is 90° wherever point C is.' (∠ACB is read as 'angle A C B'.)
y-m-30-04.thinking.0: Checking the conditions under which a claim holds
y-m-30-04.thinking.1: Making examples that satisfy the conditions from points inside the circle
y-m-30-04.thinking.2: Extending the result to the case outside the circle
y-m-30-04.prereq.0: The diameter of a circle and inscribed angles (the property that the inscribed angle on a semicircle is a right angle)
y-m-30-04.prereq.1: The position of a point on the coordinate plane and the square of the distance between two points
y-m-30-04.prereq.2: Using the Pythagorean theorem and its converse to decide obtuse and acute angles
y-m-30-04.s.s1.prompt: What can you say now about Hyejin's statement?
y-m-30-04.s.s1.hint.0: From the words 'the inscribed angle on a semicircle', find where point C has to be.
y-m-30-04.s.s1.hint.1: Pick one point that is not on the circle (e.g. a point close to just above the origin), connect it with A and B, and estimate whether ∠ACB is greater or less than a right angle.
y-m-30-04.s.s1.o.a: She is right. If there is a diameter AB, ∠ACB is 90° wherever C is
y-m-30-04.s.s1.r.a: Think about whether the property 'the inscribed angle on a semicircle' is a condition about where the point is placed.
y-m-30-04.s.s1.o.b: She is wrong. There is no point C anywhere for which ∠ACB is 90°
y-m-30-04.s.s1.r.b: Think about whether it matches the already known property for a point C on the circle.
y-m-30-04.s.s1.o.c: I do not know yet. The property we learned can be used only when C is on the circle
y-m-30-04.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that thought about the condition under which the property applies and considered that outside its range of application more verification is needed.
y-m-30-04.s.s1.o.d: She is right. But only when the lengths of AC and BC are equal
y-m-30-04.s.s1.r.d: If AC = BC, then point C is on the y-axis. Think about whether the angle is the same at every point on it.
y-m-30-04.s.s1.explain: The property that the inscribed angle on a semicircle is 90° is about when point C is on the circle (a point other than on the diameter AB). Points inside or outside the circle must be checked separately.
y-m-30-04.s.s2.prompt: Pick points C(x, y) inside the circle whose x-coordinate and y-coordinate are both integers, and make 3 different examples in which ∠ACB is greater than a right angle (obtuse). Point C has y > 0 and is inside the circle. (Two points symmetric left and right are counted as the same example.)
y-m-30-04.s.s2.hint.0: Pick a point C, find the squares of the lengths of AC and BC, and compare their sum with the square of AB, 100.
y-m-30-04.s.s2.hint.1: Check with two points how the above comparison differs when the square of the distance from the origin to C is less than and greater than the square of 5.
y-m-30-04.s.s2.fail.c1: x and y must be integers.
y-m-30-04.s.s2.fail.c2: Point C must be at a place where y > 0.
y-m-30-04.s.s2.ok.c3: Point C is inside the circle (∠ACB is obtuse).
y-m-30-04.s.s2.fail.c3: Point C is not inside the circle. Check whether the square of the distance from the origin to C is less than 25.
y-m-30-04.s.s2.explain: For example, if C(0, 1), then AC² = 26 and BC² = 26, and the sum is 52, which is less than AB² = 100, so ∠ACB is obtuse. C(3, 4) is a point on the circle, so it is a right angle, and C(4, 4) is outside the circle, so AC² + BC² = 114 > 100, which makes it acute.
y-m-30-04.s.s3.prompt: At a point C outside the circle (y > 0), is ∠ACB greater or less than 90°? Pick a point and check with numbers, and organize and write how ∠ACB changes depending on the position of point C (inside the circle, on the circle, outside the circle).
y-m-30-04.s.s3.hint.0: Pick a point outside the circle and make the same comparison as in s2 (AC² + BC² and AB²).
y-m-30-04.s.s3.hint.1: Write in a table how the result of that comparison differs inside the circle, on the circle, and outside the circle.
y-m-30-04.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. The point outside the circle (...)
y-m-30-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: At the point I chose, did I directly compare the sizes of AC², BC², and AB²?
y-m-30-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did I talk about all three cases: inside, on, and outside the circle?
y-m-30-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did I say the direction of change, such as 'as the point moves farther away'?
y-m-30-04.s.s3.model.0: Looking at the point C(4, 4) outside the circle, AC²=81+16=97, BC²=1+16=17, and the sum 114 is greater than AB²=100, so ∠ACB is an acute angle less than 90°. In summary, inside the circle it is obtuse, on the circle it is a right angle, and outside the circle it is acute.
y-m-30-04.s.s3.model.1: The point (6, 1) outside the circle has a squared distance of 37 from the origin, which is greater than 25. Then ∠ACB is less than 90°. The farther C moves from AB, the narrower the angle gets, and it is exactly 90° only on the circle.

y-m-30-05.title: Is a rhombus always inscribed in a circle?
y-m-30-05.topic: The sum of opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle
y-m-30-05.goal: Use the fact that the sum of two opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle is 180° as the standard to check the belief that 'a rhombus is always inscribed', and make several sets of four angles of quadrilaterals that satisfy the conditions.
y-m-30-05.material: A quadrilateral whose four vertices are all on one circle is called a 'quadrilateral inscribed in a circle'. In a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle, the sum of the sizes of two opposite angles is 180°. Jiho thinks, 'A rhombus, whose four sides are all equal, is always inscribed in a circle.' (In a rhombus, opposite angles are equal in size.)
y-m-30-05.thinking.0: Using a property as a standard for judgment
y-m-30-05.thinking.1: Making several examples that satisfy the constraints (sum of opposite angles, not a parallelogram)
y-m-30-05.thinking.2: Finding the special case in which the claim holds
y-m-30-05.prereq.0: The sum of the four angles of a quadrilateral is 360°
y-m-30-05.prereq.1: In a rhombus, opposite angles are equal in size
y-m-30-05.prereq.2: The property that the sum of two opposite angles of a quadrilateral inscribed in a circle is 180° (assume it can be used in this task)
y-m-30-05.s.s1.prompt: There is a rhombus ABCD with ∠A = 70°. Can this rhombus be inscribed in a circle?
y-m-30-05.s.s1.hint.0: First write what relationship there must be between opposite angles if the quadrilateral is inscribed.
y-m-30-05.s.s1.hint.1: Find the size of the angle opposite ∠A in this rhombus, and check whether the relationship above holds.
y-m-30-05.s.s1.o.a: It is inscribed. The four sides are equal, so the four vertices lie on a circle
y-m-30-05.s.s1.r.a: Think about whether having equal side lengths and having the vertices lie on one circle are the same thing.
y-m-30-05.s.s1.o.b: It is not inscribed. The sum of ∠A and its opposite ∠C is 140°
y-m-30-05.s.s1.r.b: This is a judgment that checked whether the sum of the two opposite angles is 180°.
y-m-30-05.s.s1.o.c: It is inscribed. Because the sum of the four angles is 360°
y-m-30-05.s.s1.r.c: The sum of the four angles is 360° in every quadrilateral. Think about whether it is a standard that can decide whether it is inscribed.
y-m-30-05.s.s1.o.d: You cannot judge unless you know ∠B
y-m-30-05.s.s1.r.d: Think about whether you can judge even if just one of the pairs of opposite angles is not 180°.
y-m-30-05.s.s1.explain: In a rhombus, ∠C = ∠A = 70°, so ∠A + ∠C = 140° ≠ 180°. If it were inscribed, the sum of the two opposite angles would have to be 180°, but it is not, so this rhombus is not inscribed in a circle.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.prompt: Make 3 different sets of the sizes of the four angles (in degrees, integers) of a quadrilateral ABCD inscribed in a circle that is not a parallelogram. The opposite angles are A and C, and B and D. (Ones that only differ in order are counted as the same example.)
y-m-30-05.s.s2.hint.0: First decide ∠A, then decide ∠C. Is there a relationship between opposite angles?
y-m-30-05.s.s2.hint.1: Decide ∠B and ∠D in the same way, then check the sum of the four angles and that ∠A and ∠C are not equal.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.ok.c1: All four angles are positive integers.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.fail.c1: All four angles must be integers (in degrees) greater than 0.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.ok.c2: The sum of the four angles is 360°.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.fail.c2: The sum of the four angles is not 360°.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.ok.c3: The sum of each pair of opposite angles is 180°.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.fail.c3: The sum of the opposite angles (A and C, B and D) is not 180°.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.ok.c4: The opposite angles are different from each other, so it is not a parallelogram.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.fail.c4: If ∠A and ∠C are equal, it could be a parallelogram. Make them different from each other.
y-m-30-05.s.s2.explain: If you set the sum of ∠A and ∠C and the sum of ∠B and ∠D each to 180°, the sum of the four angles automatically becomes 360°. As long as ∠A ≠ ∠C, it is not a parallelogram. (70°, 80°, 110°, 100°) and (60°, 90°, 120°, 90°) are examples.
y-m-30-05.s.s3.prompt: If there is a rhombus for which Jiho's thought 'a rhombus is always inscribed in a circle' is right, what kind of rhombus would it be? Write the reason too.
y-m-30-05.s.s3.hint.0: Call one angle of the rhombus x, write the opposite angle as x, and write what value the sum of the two angles must be.
y-m-30-05.s.s3.hint.1: Describe in words the shape of the rhombus that has that x.
y-m-30-05.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If one angle is x, ...
y-m-30-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you use the fact that when one angle of a rhombus is x, the opposite angle is also x?
y-m-30-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you say how x is determined (2x = 180°)?
y-m-30-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you make clear the conclusion that it is not every rhombus?
y-m-30-05.s.s3.model.0: A square. If one angle is 90°, the sum of opposite angles is 90°+90°=180°, so it can be inscribed in a circle.
y-m-30-05.s.s3.model.1: Only a rhombus whose angles are all right angles, that is, a square, is possible. Opposite angles of a rhombus are equal, so if one angle is x, then 2x=180°, so x=90°.

y-m-30-06.title: Is the area of a triangle with two sides 6 and 10 determined?
y-m-30-06.topic: The area of a triangle (two sides and the included angle)
y-m-30-06.goal: Learn that the lengths of two sides alone do not determine the area of a triangle, tell apart what extra information determines it, and explain that there are triangles with the same area but different shapes.
y-m-30-06.thinking.0: Judging whether the information is sufficient
y-m-30-06.thinking.1: Finding all the answers that satisfy the same condition
y-m-30-06.thinking.2: Explaining that shapes differ for the same area
y-m-30-06.prereq.0: The expression for the area of a triangle using two sides and the sine of the angle between them (½ × product of two sides × sin(included angle))
y-m-30-06.prereq.2: The congruence conditions for triangles (once the three sides are determined, the triangle is determined as one)
y-m-30-06.s.s1.prompt: In addition to AB = 6 and AC = 10, choose all the cases in which the area of the triangle is determined as one value when one of the following is known.
y-m-30-06.s.s1.hint.0: For each piece of information, separately work out whether only one triangle can be made or several.
y-m-30-06.s.s1.hint.1: For 'it is acute', find two or more possible values of ∠A and compare the areas.
y-m-30-06.s.s1.r.a: Think about whether the value of sin A varies in several ways even within the range of acute angles.
y-m-30-06.s.s1.o.b: The length of BC is 8 cm
y-m-30-06.s.s1.r.b: Think about whether the triangle is determined as one when all three sides are determined.
y-m-30-06.s.s1.r.c: Think about whether, if you know the included angle, you can find the area directly with the formula.
y-m-30-06.s.s1.o.d: The triangle is not an isosceles triangle
y-m-30-06.s.s1.r.d: Think about whether this information determines ∠A as one value.
y-m-30-06.s.s1.explain: If you know the included angle ∠A = 60°, the area is determined as ½×6×10×sin 60° = 15√3 ≈ 26.0 cm². If BC = 8, the three sides are determined so the triangle is determined as one (in fact 6, 8, 10 is a triangle with a right angle at B, so the area is ½×6×8 = 24 cm²), and the area is also determined as one value. 'It is acute' or 'it is not an isosceles triangle' does not determine ∠A as one value.
y-m-30-06.s.s2.prompt: For the area to be exactly 15 cm², what must ∠A be? Choose all the possible ones.
y-m-30-06.s.s2.hint.0: For each candidate ∠A, calculate the value of ½×6×10×sin A and compare it with 15.
y-m-30-06.s.s2.r.a: If you did not check what the sin value is for an obtuse angle, this is an easy value to miss.
y-m-30-06.s.s2.r.b: If you calculate the area for a right angle directly, you can check whether it comes out to 15.
y-m-30-06.s.s2.r.c: This is a value for which you checked the area using sin 30° = 1/2.
y-m-30-06.s.s2.r.d: If you calculate the area with the value of sin 60°, you can check whether it comes out to 15.
y-m-30-06.s.s2.explain: Area = ½×6×10×sin A = 30 sin A = 15 gives sin A = 1/2. Between 0° and 180°, there are two angles with sin A = 1/2: 30° and 150°. At 90° the area is 30, and at 60° it is about 26.0.
y-m-30-06.s.s3.hint.0: Compare which side is the longest in each of the two triangles.
y-m-30-06.s.s3.hint.1: Take AC as the base and compare the heights drawn from B in the two cases.
y-m-30-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you explain what differs between the two triangles with numbers (the length of BC, etc.)?
y-m-30-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you separate the reason the areas are the same (the height is the same, the sin value is the same) from the reason the shapes are different?
y-m-30-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say which of the two is the obtuse triangle?
y-m-30-06.s.s3.model.0: If ∠A=30°, ∠A is acute and BC is about 5.7 cm, but at 150° it is obtuse and BC is about 15.5 cm, much longer. Even if the area is the same, 15, the shape is different.
y-m-30-06.s.s3.model.1: In both, if you take AC as the base 10, the height drawn from B is the same, 3 cm, so the areas are the same. But at 150°, B is off toward the extension of AC, so the shape is different.

y-m-30-07.title: Is the distance between two parallel chords determined as one value?
y-m-30-07.topic: Chords of a circle and the distance to the center
y-m-30-07.goal: Find the distance from the center to a chord, and judge and write that the answer is complete only when you consider both the case where two parallel chords are on the same side of the center and the case where they are on opposite sides.
y-m-30-07.material: In a circle O with radius 13 cm, there are a chord AB of length 24 cm and a chord CD of length 10 cm. The two chords are parallel to each other. No figure is given. You want to find the distance between the two chords. (The perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to a chord bisects that chord.)
y-m-30-07.thinking.0: Checking the calculation of intermediate values
y-m-30-07.thinking.1: Finding the assumption placed implicitly in a solution
y-m-30-07.thinking.2: Writing an answer that depends on conditions (splitting into cases)
y-m-30-07.prereq.0: The fact that the perpendicular drawn from the center of a circle to a chord bisects that chord
y-m-30-07.prereq.1: The relation among the three sides of a right triangle
y-m-30-07.prereq.2: The sum and difference of distances
y-m-30-07.s.s1.prompt: How far is each chord from the center O of the circle?
y-m-30-07.s.s1.hint.0: Describe in words the triangle whose vertices are the foot of the perpendicular, one endpoint of the chord, and the center O, and find where the right angle is.
y-m-30-07.s.s1.hint.1: After deciding which side of that triangle is the longest, write the expression that finds the remaining side from the two known lengths.
y-m-30-07.s.s1.o.a: 12 cm to AB, 5 cm to CD
y-m-30-07.s.s1.r.a: You may have thought that the longer the chord, the farther it is from the center. Make a right triangle with half the chord and the radius to check.
y-m-30-07.s.s1.o.b: 1 cm to AB, 8 cm to CD
y-m-30-07.s.s1.r.b: You may have found it by simply subtracting half the chord from the radius. Check which side is the hypotenuse.
y-m-30-07.s.s1.o.c: 5 cm to AB, 12 cm to CD
y-m-30-07.s.s1.r.c: This is a value that used the fact that the perpendicular from the center to a chord passes through the midpoint of the chord.
y-m-30-07.s.s1.o.d: √313 cm to AB, √194 cm to CD
y-m-30-07.s.s1.r.d: You may have added the square of half the chord to the square of the radius. Check which side is the hypotenuse.
y-m-30-07.s.s1.explain: The foot of the perpendicular from O to AB is the midpoint of AB, and in the right triangle formed by the half length 12 and the radius 13, the distance is √(13² − 12²) = 5. For CD, the half length is 5, so √(13² − 5²) = 12. The longer the chord, the closer to the center.
y-m-30-07.s.s2.prompt: Below is a solution that found the distance between the two chords. Choose the line that has an assumption made without a reason. Count the line numbers from 1.
y-m-30-07.s.s2.line.0: The distance from the center O to AB is 5 cm, and the distance to CD is 12 cm.
y-m-30-07.s.s2.line.1: The two chords are parallel, so the perpendiculars from O to the two chords lie on one line.
y-m-30-07.s.s2.line.4: So the answer is only 7 cm.
y-m-30-07.s.s3.prompt: Draw the case where the two chords are on opposite sides of the center O. Find the distance then, and write how the answer to this problem should be written.
y-m-30-07.s.s3.hint.0: Change the assumption in line 3 of the solution and draw the two chords on opposite sides of O.
y-m-30-07.s.s3.hint.1: In that case, write in words how to combine the distances 5 and 12 from O to the two chords to get the distance between the two chords.
y-m-30-07.s.s3.placeholder: e.g. If they are on opposite sides, ...
y-m-30-07.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you say how you found the distance for the opposite sides (how you combined 5 and 12)?
y-m-30-07.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write both the same side (7 cm) and the opposite side (17 cm) as answers?
y-m-30-07.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you say the reason that without a figure the positions are not determined?
y-m-30-07.s.s3.model.0: If they are on opposite sides, it is 5+12=17 cm. So if the two chords are on the same side of O it is 7 cm, and if on opposite sides it is 17 cm, and since there is no figure, both cases, 7 cm or 17 cm, are answers.
y-m-30-07.s.s3.model.1: If O is between them, add 5 and 12 to get 17 cm. If on the same side, 7 cm. The problem has no condition about position, so I should write that there are two answers (7 cm, 17 cm).

y-m-30-08.title: The longest stick that fits in a box
y-m-30-08.topic: The diagonal of a rectangular box (using the Pythagorean theorem in three dimensions)
y-m-30-08.goal: When finding the length of a segment in a solid, use the fact that the diagonal of the base and the height form a right angle, make boxes in which the diagonal length is a natural number in several ways, and judge whether a stick fits.
y-m-30-08.material: There is an empty rectangular box 3 cm wide, 4 cm deep, and 12 cm high. You want to put a very thin stick that does not bend entirely inside this box. Ignore the thickness of the box, and assume the inside measurements are the same as the outside measurements. You want to find the length of the longest stick that can fit inside the box.
y-m-30-08.thinking.0: Finding the wrong line in a solution with an error
y-m-30-08.thinking.1: Making several boxes that satisfy the constraints
y-m-30-08.thinking.2: Judging by comparing a result with the length of a stick
y-m-30-08.prereq.0: The diagonal length of a rectangle (the Pythagorean theorem)
y-m-30-08.prereq.1: The positional relation of edges and faces of a rectangular box (the base and the height are perpendicular)
y-m-30-08.s.s1.prompt: Below is a solution in which a student found the length of the longest stick. Choose the one wrong line. Count the line numbers from 1.
y-m-30-08.s.s1.hint.0: Describe in words how the stick lies slanted from one edge of the box to the opposite top edge, and look at what angle the 5 and the 12 in line 3 make with each other.
y-m-30-08.s.s1.hint.1: Draw the triangle formed by the two segments of 5 cm and 12 cm and the stick. Check using the relation between the sides of a triangle whether the three side lengths could be 5, 12, 17.
y-m-30-08.s.s1.line.0: The base is a rectangle 3 by 4.
y-m-30-08.s.s1.line.1: The length of the diagonal of the base is 3² + 4² = 25, so it is 5.
y-m-30-08.s.s1.line.2: The stick lies in the shape connecting the base diagonal 5 and the height 12, so 5 + 12 = 17.
y-m-30-08.s.s1.line.3: So the longest stick is 17 cm.
y-m-30-08.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the problem. The stick passes slanted from one corner of the base to the opposite top corner, so the diagonal of the base (5) and the height (12) are perpendicular to each other, and the stick is the hypotenuse of the right triangle that has those two as its sides. The hypotenuse is not the sum of the two sides but the square root of the sum of their squares, so it is shorter. So the 17 cm in line 4 is also wrong. Calculated correctly, √(5² + 12²) = 13 cm.
y-m-30-08.s.s2.prompt: Among rectangular boxes whose width a, depth b, and height c are all natural numbers from 1 to 12, make 3 different boxes in which the length of the longest stick that fits inside is also a natural number. (Boxes with a, b, c only in a different order are the same box.)
y-m-30-08.s.s2.hint.0: Decide two of the three lengths and find the square of the base diagonal, then change the height and check whether the total sum becomes the square of some number.
y-m-30-08.s.s2.hint.1: Compare the boxes you found with the original 3, 4, 12, and try in order starting from small numbers in the same way.
y-m-30-08.s.s2.ok.c1: The three lengths are natural numbers from 1 to 12.
y-m-30-08.s.s2.fail.c1: The width, depth, and height must be natural numbers from 1 to 12.
y-m-30-08.s.s2.ok.c2: The length of the longest stick is a natural number.
y-m-30-08.s.s2.fail.c2: The length of the longest stick (the square root of the sum of the squares of the three lengths) is not a natural number.
y-m-30-08.s.s2.explain: For example, (1, 2, 2) gives √9 = 3, (2, 3, 6) gives √49 = 7, (4, 4, 7) gives √81 = 9, and (2, 4, 4) gives √36 = 6. The original box (3, 4, 12) gives √169 = 13, so it is one of the boxes that satisfy this condition.
y-m-30-08.s.s3.prompt: You put a stick in the box with width 3, depth 4, and height 12. What is the fitting relationship between the length of the stick and the box? (13 cm is the length of the longest stick.)
y-m-30-08.s.s3.hint.0: With a 13 cm stick lying along the diagonal, describe in words what happens to its length if you move one end slightly inward.
y-m-30-08.s.s3.hint.1: For each option, make a table by splitting into when the stick is longer than 13, when it is 13, and when it is shorter than 13.
y-m-30-08.s.s3.o.a: A stick of 13.1 cm also fits if you lay it slanted
y-m-30-08.s.s3.r.a: Think about whether a stick longer than the longest stick's length can fit.
y-m-30-08.s.s3.o.b: Every stick longer than 12 cm does not fit
y-m-30-08.s.s3.r.b: You may have taken 12 as the limit because the height is the longest edge. Think about whether a slanted segment can be longer than an edge.
y-m-30-08.s.s3.o.c: Every stick of 13 cm or less fits and 13.1 cm does not fit
y-m-30-08.s.s3.r.c: This is a judgment that considered together the length of the longest segment and whether sticks shorter than it fit.
y-m-30-08.s.s3.o.d: Only a 13 cm stick fits and a 12.8 cm stick does not fit
y-m-30-08.s.s3.r.d: You may have thought a shorter stick cannot be put in. Think about what happens if you move one end of the stick.
y-m-30-08.s.s3.explain: The longest segment that can be placed inside the box is 13 cm (the diagonal), so every stick of 13 cm or less can be put in, and a 13.1 cm stick does not fit. A stick longer than 12 cm can also fit if laid slanted.
